why: It is the page read for a city's gates, and not only its ward gates, being barred from dusk, which is why a traveler arriving late stayed outside. It quotes its classical passages without saying which edition, and its detailed account is of one capital, Tang Chang'an, with the later dynasties covered in a sentence; it asks about leaving a city at night rather than entering one, and that a county town's gate kept the same hours is our extension of it, not its statement.

It is the page read for a walled Chinese city that took the rivers along its flanks as its moat - the Song layout "relying on the rivers as the moat", the Qianlong-era county gazetteer's "the encircling rivers serving as its moat" - with a single landward side. It quotes the gazetteer through a 2015 newspaper report and the layout phrase through a site-survey report, and Chongqing is a hill city whose walls stand on river cliffs, so it shows the river standing in for the moat, not how a lowland river city's dug moat met its river; it nowhere compares the river's defensive worth with a dug moat's.

It is the page read for how Edo-period timber was handled at the water: floated in, worked and stored afloat in timber ponds, the kiba names across Japan lying on the sea or a river because logs came by sea or were floated down from upstream. It is centered on one great city's specialized timber district, not on a provincial river landing, and it says nothing of piers, of stone, or of how a mixed river port was laid out. Its two claims are not equally supported: the account of timber floated and stored in ponds cites the Tokyo Metropolitan Library's modern commentary on its copy of the Edo Meisho Zue (1834-36), so it rests on a library's reading of a period work, not on the work itself; no date for the quarter's founding is taken from the article; and the statement that kiba place names lie on the sea or a river because logs came by sea or were floated downstream carries no reference and is the article's own generalization.

It names the two bamboo beatings (笞 and 杖) as statutory punishments of the Qing code, which is what the justice works' "beating" is. It defines each punishment and says nothing of where or before whom a beating was carried out, so the yamen courtyard as its place rests on other pages or on our reading.

It says that the Edo intendants of the Kanto lived in Edo and went out to their villages only for land surveys, harvest inspections, tours of inspection and serious incidents, which is the historical form of an official seen rarely in the countryside. It is a tertiary summary, and the article carries Wikipedia's banner saying it cites no or too few sources, with no citation on this sentence. The sentence concerns the Kanto intendants of the shogunate's own lands in particular, not the daimyo domains. It says those intendants governed through contact with their tetsuke, the staff officers under them, so what was rare was a visit from the intendant himself, not all contact with the state. It gives no count of visits a year, so any frequency is our estimate. It is also the page read for the size of an intendant's staff: about ten shogunal retainers (tetsuki) and a few locally hired clerks (tedai), and at one late-Edo intendancy a single intendant, three tetsuki and ten tedai. Its one scholarly citation (Nakata 2002) supports only its history of how the intendancy became a salaried office, from 1657 through the Kyōhō reforms (1725), and both staff figures are uncited; the Gojō count is given as hearsay ("it is said"). The counts are of officials and clerks only: the article says menial ashigaru and chūgen served beside them, so more hands worked at the office than the figures give. Its two figures do not agree on the mix (about ten tetsuki and a few tedai, against three tetsuki and ten tedai at Gojō). They are for the shogunate's intendancies, which varied in size: one staff ran a district usually of several tens of thousands of koku (Gojō's was 70,000), not a single town. Intendants near the Kantō lived in Edo and came only for surveys, inspections, tours and serious incidents.

It describes how long an ox-drawn train halted at midday and what the animals did while it rested, the one readable account found of a draft team's rest at a stop. It is nineteenth-century America, not East Asia, and an emigrant train rather than a post-station; we take only what an ox team at a halt did, and only as a rough bound. Its "an hour or so" is a generalization, and it says a train might stay several hours in hot weather. The length of the halt was set by the wagon leader to fit the day's travel, not by the animals alone. Its oxen grazed open range at camp stops in open country on a trek of months, not in a town yard where animals are fed fodder.

It gives the towpath's overall length and its forms, which set the scale and shape of the hauling path our river capital draws. It carries no dimensions of the deck, and its length and forms describe the towpath as it survives, whose fabric is later than the Tang institution.

It is a general account by a specialist of what homestead groves were for and how they varied, which bears on how big a village's groves were only so far as to say that their form, size and species varied. It names regions only as examples (the tsuiji-matsu of the Hikawa plain in Shimane, the zelkova and oak groves of the Kantō plain). It describes the groves as they stood in twentieth-century Japan, already declining as farm households fell; only its note on the related village woods, whose grown trees needed the domain's leave to fell, reaches back to the Edo period. So it shows the form lasted into living memory, and dates no grove's form or size to the era we draw.

It gives the ideal-type layout of a Japanese village - houses at the center, fields around them, hill and wild land beyond - and says when its outer boundary, the edge of the hill and wild land, became clear: gradually through the self-governing medieval village, and then fixed by the land surveys and village partition at the start of the Edo period. The entry never names woods; that a village's woods stood in that outer ring of hill and wild land is this project's reading. It is an ideal type, as the author says, not a survey of real villages. Its hedge ("it is thought") falls only on the outer boundary having once been unclear. And it describes the Japanese village only: bounds fixed by the Edo land survey are a Japanese institution, and it says nothing of how Chinese villages were bounded.

It says in plain words why hill-land boundaries between villages were unclear, and what the hill land was used for (grass and brush for paddy manure, and firewood), in an Edo-period dispute over shared hill forest in Mino. The statement that forest boundaries were vague because of broken terrain, steep valleys and hills with no view is the writers' general remark about "old times", not a finding drawn from this dispute's records, and it describes steep mountain country rather than gentle woodland near a village. It is about one pair of domains in the Kiso valley, and cites no documents by name.

It names the resting plot this record asks about and gives two reasons for the rest, poor soil and short water. It describes the Heian period, not the medieval village or the early modern one. That the rest came in strict alternate years is disputed elsewhere: one historian's review treats the resting land as ground idle for that one year, and an unsourced encyclopedia note denies that alternate-year farming existed at all.

It is the one page read that says where the resting land lay: usually (its word) mixed in among the cropped land rather than in a solid tract, and, while resting, left unmarked and grazed in common by cattle and horses. It describes a word found in Heian poetry and the fields of that age. The Nihon kokugo daijiten entry on the same page gives thin soil as the reason for resting the land, which marks it as an early, low-yield practice and not one of the settled village of later centuries. It says nothing of which plots of a village's paddy were the ones to rest.

It separates paddy lost for good from a plot resting between crops, and its note on kataarashi is the one dissent read from the alternate-year definition. That note gives no source of its own and is weighed as an opinion, not a finding. It also contradicts the article's own main text, which describes kataarashi as poor land cultivated and left fallow in turn, with the fallow grazed. The article therefore carries both readings, and only its uncited note dissents. The article covers the ancient and medieval periods only.

It is a signed encyclopedia entry covering both the bund's role and its yearly upkeep, which this record needs. It gives no width. "From of old" is its only reach into the past, and it gives no period of its own. Some of its detail is modern and is not drawn: it asks the bund to carry "people and work machines", treats seepage through the bund as a loss of irrigation water, and names concrete and vinyl bunds. The uses and the azenuri it describes are long-standing hand practice, and we use it for those alone.

A season word records a task farmers did at a set time of year. The entry places azenuri before rice planting, and its verses show the task in poetry. It does not date its verses. Keikō was an Edo-period poet of Bashō's circle, so his verse shows the task before the modern era; Murakami Kijō (1865-1938) wrote in the modern era. Its "late spring" is the haiku almanac's season, fixed only as "before rice planting" and not as a calendar date, and the date of that work varied by region. It notes that the work is now done by machine.

It says azenuri was done by hand with the hoe, before machines, but gives no date for that practice; the Nogu benriron line it quotes is early modern but secondhand, and speaks of hoes in general, not of azenuri. So it shows the hoe as the tool of traditional Japanese azenuri, not that the practice as described is Edo-period. It contradicts itself on the pulling hoe, calling it once a hoe for moving soil and once one for deep tillage. It is cited only for the hoe and the Nogu benriron line.

It gives the drain's other name (nakaboshi), its season and its purpose, and the usual length of about a week; it does not say which name is older. It is a stub whose farming paragraph rests on one prefectural extension answer (Yamagata). The week and the purposes it gives (air to the roots, holding back useless stems) are modern extension advice. The drain is older than that - Edo-period farming manuals describe it - but before the war it was done only in some districts with plenty of water and fields that could be drained, and it became general only after the war, with drainage works and chemical fertilizer (Horikawa, Yoshida and Masumoto, 2011). So for our setting it is a local practice, not a universal one, and the week is a modern figure.

It states the mechanism by which the reed beds were kept open - cutting the reed stops old reed from building up into soil on which willow and other trees then grow, and burning the bed makes it harder for trees to take - as a practice people have long carried out on the lake to get good reed for blinds and roofs. It gives no date for the practice, no measurement and no frequency (it never says the reed was cut or burned every year), it describes Lake Biwa's shore rather than a village's marsh toe, and so it supports that cutting keeps trees out of a reed bed, not how any particular settlement managed its margin.

It gives the Chinese name and definition of the simplest crossing, though not Chinese evidence for it, since its sources are American and British. Its wording counts a single board as the same object as a single trunk, which matters for how our plank glyph is read, but that reading is the editor's: the 1915 source it cites speaks only of logs "in natural condition or hewn". It speaks of narrow rivers and gorges rather than farm ditches.

It states the condition that decides between a bare intake and a weir, and it describes the earliest and simplest weirs, which were built on small streams - the scale of a hamlet's brook. It gives no dates for most of its general statements, no dimensions, and no count of how many intakes took each form. Neither pictured weir is from the setting's era: the Kodera weir is an excavated work of the early Kofun period (about the 3rd-4th century), far earlier, and the grass weir is a present-day survival photographed in Saga, which the caption says is used where an agreement with users downstream forbids a permanent weir - a modern observation of an old form, not a dated record of it.

It corroborates the two-form division of intakes and gives the one regional statement read about which form an area used: the ancient Ningxia intakes on the Yellow River were all damless. Every example on the page is a large state or prefectural canal (the Zhibo and Zhang canals, Dujiangyan, the Ningxia canals), so the two-form division is a modern engineering classification of great works, carried to a hamlet's brook only by analogy; Ningxia's are large canals off a great river, not a hamlet's brook. "Damless" there means no dam across the river, not no work in it: the same page says the Qing built stone-and-brushwood guide dikes out into the Yellow River at those mouths, one 450 zhang long. It hedges its dates (the Qin River canal was built "about" the Qin; its wooden gate was rebuilt in stone under the Cao Wei).

It says the intake gate of the Western Han Langtang Canal was a timber structure, and that the mouth of the Eastern Han Bian Canal was later given a stone gate - two different works, not one gate rebuilt - which is the material of an intake mouth where one was built. It is an unsigned reference entry on China Agriculture Press's knowledge platform that gives one line to the point and cites no period text, so it carries the material and nothing finer. It concerns great state canals of the Han period, not village works, and gives no dimensions.

It describes the one means of shutting a water opening read in this pass: boards slotted into cut grooves, added or removed to set the water held. The Mulan weir is a large river work, not a village intake. It describes the weir as it stands today and does not date its gate grooves or boards; the weir has been repaired and altered over nine centuries (its 32 openings are now 28), so it shows the method at this weir, not that these grooves are Song work. The same article's Tang-era Tashan weir, whose body its editor calls a stop-log chamber, is an older instance of the form.

It sets out the competing explanations for the ban - the defense of Edo and Sunpu, the river's own violence, the profits of the crossing towns - so that this page can state the motive as argued rather than certain.

It places the village's river on its east side, flowing past it - a one-bank siting, and a check on travel pages that describe the same river as running through the village. The sentence on the river carries no footnote of its own. It describes the present-day village, whose water has been changed since (a lake was dug in 2007). It is silent on the two channels (水圳) that other accounts say carry the river's water through the village's streets, so it shows the river on one side of the village, not a village that draws nothing from it. The river is a 19 km watercourse, larger than a hamlet's brook.

It gives two reasons a paddy did not carry a winter crop - no fertilizer to spare away from the crowded districts, and a wet paddy that barley cannot stand - which is what makes the winter crop a per-settlement matter. The fertilizer sentence is set in Japan's medieval period and rests on one cited book (Yokoi and Amino, 2003); the wet-paddy sentence cites nothing, so that reason stands on the encyclopedia alone until a period or scholarly source carries it; and the page gives no Edo figures.

It gives one form of the rick, straw stacked in a cylinder round a central pole, and says the shape varied from region to region; and it says what the straw went to, compost and straw goods (rice bags and rope), which is our reason for drawing the rick still standing into the winter - the entry itself does not say how long it stood. It gives no date, place or measurement, the pole-centered cylinder is one regional form among several, and its one example verse is of the twentieth century (Matsumoto Takashi, 1906-1956), so nothing here dates the rick to the Edo period or earlier, and filing the rick under late autumn says when the rick is seen, not how long it stood.

It says ridge culture was shaped to the ground it was on - higher ridges and deeper furrows for drainage in the rainy, low-lying south - and sums the practice up as suiting the measure to the place, which supports reading the direction of rows as a matter of the land. Some of its quotations of period books and its centimetre figures (a "垄欲广，沟欲深" credited to Fan Shengzhi, a "凡种五谷，先须起垄" credited to the Qimin Yaoshu, ridge heights credited to the Nongzheng Quanshu) could not be traced to those texts. Its southern high-ridge form is told as a Wei-Jin migration story without a period source, so it carries the general point and not a figure or a quotation. It says nothing of which way the rows ran, and the "suit it to the place" phrase is its summing-up of ridge culture as a whole.

It describes a Japanese homestead grove that is kept today as a clipped wall of a single species: black pines on the west and north of the house, cut to a set height every four or five years, and it gives the grove's traditional origin in pines and bamboo planted to bind an earth bank raised against floods. The origin is given as what is said rather than as documented history, with no date. Some of what it says is modern: it gives protecting the pines from pine wilt, a twentieth-century pest, as one reason for the pruning. By its own account, the bank was first planted with bamboo as well as pine, so the single-species wall is the grove as it stands now, not necessarily as it was first planted. That this is the only Japanese homestead grove of one species is our reading, not the page's.
It states that the square tulou is the most widespread form, the fact this page uses to show that the round fortress-house is the exception even where it is famous.

It states in one sentence that the reed was long a part of daily life and that the beds were kept healthy by cutting in winter and burning in spring. It names no era for the practice, and the schedule it announces (cutting in early December, burning from late February to early March) is Takashima city's present-day conservation program, run with local groups. It speaks of Lake Biwa's reed beds only.

It dates the dike-pond types - fruit dikes first in the mid-Ming, mulberry dikes replacing them from the late Ming and early Qing - and says which livestock belonged to which district, pigs to the dike-pond district and ducks to the sand fields. Some of its types (the cane, rice and fan-palm dikes) are named for the Ming-Qing period with no date of their own, and it gives no shares of households or of ponds.
